title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Restrictive lung disease encompasses a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by reduced lung volumes and impaired compliance, resulting in compromised gas exchange and increased work of breathing. Intrinsic causes, such as interstitial lung diseases, involve fibrotic or inflammatory processes within the lung parenchyma. In contrast, extrinsic causes arise from factors outside the lungs, including obesity, neuromuscular disorders, chest wall abnormalities, and pleural pathology. Common clinical manifestations include progressive exertional dyspnea, reduced exercise tolerance, and chronic cough, with advanced disease leading to hypoxemia, respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension, and cor pulmonale. Diagnosis is established primarily through pulmonary function testing, demonstrating decreased total lung capacity with a preserved or increased forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity ratio. High-resolution imaging, histopathology, and genetic testing further support diagnosis and classification. Prognosis varies widely by etiology, ranging from reversible conditions such as pleural effusion to progressive fibrotic diseases such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, which carries a median survival of 3 to 5 years.

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Participants completing this activity gain a comprehensive understanding of the diagnostic evaluation, prognosis, and management strategies for restrictive lung disease, emphasizing evidence-based application of antifibrotic therapy, immunosuppression, pulmonary rehabilitation, and supportive care. Clinicians enhance competence in distinguishing between intrinsic and extrinsic causes and tailoring management to the underlying pathophysiology. Collaboration with an interprofessional team, including pulmonologists, primary care clinicians, nurses, pharmacists, cardiologists, nutritionists, neurologists, and palliative care specialists, optimizes patient outcomes through coordinated care. Interdisciplinary involvement ensures the timely recognition of complications, the appropriate initiation of advanced therapies, and an improved quality of life for patients with progressive or terminal disease. By integrating knowledge across specialties, clinicians strengthen decision-making and deliver patient-centered care that improves long-term outcomes in restrictive lung disease.

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Differentiate intrinsic from extrinsic causes of restrictive lung disease based on clinical presentation, pulmonary function testing, and imaging findings to improve diagnostic accuracy. Assess disease severity and prognosis in patients with interstitial lung diseases, including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, to guide timely initiation of antifibrotic therapy or referral for advanced care. Implement evidence-based management strategies for extrinsic restrictive disorders, including obesity, neuromuscular disease, and chest wall abnormalities, in collaboration with an interprofessional healthcare team. Apply principles of interprofessional collaboration by engaging pulmonologists, primary care clinicians, pharmacists, nutritionists, neurologists, cardiologists, and palliative care specialists to optimize long-term outcomes and quality of life in patients with restrictive lung disease. title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Introduction
content: Restrictive lung diseases are a heterogeneous set of pulmonary disorders defined by restrictive patterns on spirometry. These disorders are characterized by decreased distensibility of the lungs, which compromises lung expansion and results in reduced lung volumes, particularly a reduction in total lung capacity (TLC). [1] These functional characteristics differentiate them from obstructive pulmonary diseases, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, and bronchiolitis, which are characterized by increased resistance to flow due to partial or complete obstruction from the trachea to the terminal bronchioles. Restrictive disease accounts for approximately one-fifth of pulmonary disease, of which obstructive disease is the majority (80%). [2]

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Introduction
content: Restrictive lung diseases may be caused by the destruction of distal lung parenchyma due to infiltrates from inflammation, toxins, and mechanisms not yet fully understood (intrinsic causes) and extraparenchymal conditions (extrinsic causes). Within this group are diseases characterized by inflammatory changes involving the alveolar interstitium, with possible involvement of the peripheral bronchial structures. The conditions leading to this destruction are the interstitial lung diseases (ILDs). Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Interstitial Lung Disease ," for further information. This term refers to an umbrella of disorders characterized by diffuse cellular infiltrates in a periacinar distribution, encompassing a range of clinical presentations from occasional, self-limited inflammatory processes to severe, debilitating lung fibrosis. Other conditions originate from within the alveolus (edema, hemorrhage) and spread to interstitial structures. Whether the process begins in the interstitium or the alveolus, alteration of the lung architecture results in functional impairment.

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Introduction
content: Conversely, restrictive lung diseases may also result from disorders causing respiratory muscle dysfunction or chest wall restriction, physically impeding inspiration. Neurological or neuromuscular diseases can limit the activity of the respiratory muscles, whereas skeletal abnormalities of the thorax, abdominal distension, and pleural space abnormalities can restrict lung expansion. [3] Regardless of the intrinsic or extrinsic mechanisms, these diseases are characterized by impaired ventilatory function and respiratory failure.

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Etiology -- Pulmonary Parenchyma Diseases (Intrinsic Causes)
content: Smoking and air pollution are strong risk factors for developing ILDs like IPF. [5] [6] ILD may be grouped into diseases that lead to an increased elastic recoil (diffuse infiltrative pneumopathies and interstitial diseases) and those with alveolar filling (pneumonia). Several ILDs demonstrate strong genetic associations. For example, the MUC5B promoter gene and variants of telomere maintenance genes are risk factors for IPF, fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and rheumatoid arthritis–related ILD. [7] [8] Similarly, familial aggregation is seen in sarcoidosis with approximately a 4-fold relative risk. [9] Important genetic variations associated with the risk of ILDs and different phenotypes are listed in Table 1 below . [10] [11]

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Etiology -- Extrinsic or Extrapulmonary Diseases

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Epidemiology
content: Estimating the prevalence of restrictive diseases with precision is challenging due to their diverse range of pathological conditions, each of which can present at various clinical stages. However, intrinsic lung diseases affect between 3 and 6 per 100,000 persons in the United States. [14] The prevalence of sarcoidosis in North America has been estimated at 10 to 40 per 100,000 persons, with a higher prevalence in Sweden (64 per 100,000 persons). [15] Results from national and global population studies have demonstrated that certain groups are at a higher risk of having a restrictive pattern on spirometry. title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Epidemiology
content: Those who have specific occupational and environmental exposures are also at increased risk. Frequently encountering substances at workplaces such as asbestos, coal dust, and several other hazardous dusts can cause lung tissue alterations, leading to inflammation, tissue scarring, and a restrictive pattern on spirometry. title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Epidemiology
content: Restrictive lung diseases are rare during pregnancy, but if present, they are usually due to neuromuscular disease or kyphoscoliosis. [18] Results from an epidemiologic study showed that restrictive patterns on spirometry decreased from 7.2% to 5.4% between 1988 and 1994 and 2007 and 2010, which may be related to improved occupational safety precautions and declining cigarette smoking rates. [12]

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Pathophysiology
content: Intrinsic pulmonary restriction is most commonly characterized by inflammation of the pulmonary parenchyma, followed by collagen deposition in the interstitium, ultimately leading to pulmonary fibrosis. Over time, this progressive fibrosis thickens the alveolar septa, imposing a physical barrier to gas exchange. On pulmonary function testing (PFT), decreased diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) is observed. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Diffusing Capacity of the Lungs for Carbon Monoxide ," for more information. [1] Besides decreasing DLCO, lung tissue fibrosis decreases the compliance of the lung tissue, reducing inspiratory capacity. [19] The pathophysiology of extrapulmonary disease is due to altered mechanical function due to rib cage deformity, neurological or muscular pathologies, or pleural effusions.

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Pathophysiology -- Compliance
content: The distensibility of the respiratory system is termed compliance (C). Compliance represents the volume change produced by a change in the distending pressure, determined by the elastic forces formula: C= ΔV/ΔP

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Pathophysiology -- Compliance
content: Notably, lung compliance is independent of the thoracic cage, a semirigid casing, but the lung and thorax are systems arranged in series. Therefore, the compliance of an intact respiratory system is the sum of the compliances of both structures. Disease of the lungs, pleura, or chest wall affects compliance. Lung compliance decreases if the lung is overly rigid (in restrictive pathologies) and increases in less stiff conditions, such as emphysema. Thoracic compliance decreases with reduced distensibility of the rib cage (obesity, kyphoscoliosis).

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Pathophysiology -- Compliance
content: The combined compliance of the thorax and lungs is 110 mL/cm H 2 O, whereas the compliance alone is approximately 200 mL/cm H 2 O. Decreased compliance from intrapulmonary or extrapulmonary causes results in greater pressure generation and energy requirements from the respiratory muscles for any given tidal volume. [19] These changes in respiratory physiology eventually lead to tissue hypoxia and dyspnea.

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Pathophysiology -- Hypoxemia
content: Hypoxemia (PaO 2 <60 mm Hg), with or without hypercapnia (PaCO 2 >45 mm Hg), can be a consequence of lung damage and an expression of respiratory failure. In restrictive diseases, hypoxia occurs through different mechanisms depending on the type of disease. In intrinsic conditions, alterations in the gas diffusion with a ventilation-perfusion ratio mismatch contribute to hypoxia. This process leads to an increased intrapulmonary shunt, defined as the portion of the pulmonary blood flow that bypasses the alveoli or perfuses unventilated alveoli and does not participate in gas exchange. Conversely, hypoventilation and respiratory pump failure are prominent in extrinsic disease.

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Pathophysiology -- Functional Characteristics
content: Functional characteristics of a restrictive pattern on PFTs include decreased TLC and forced vital capacity (FVC). Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Pulmonary Function Tests and Thoracic Cage Abnormalities ," for more information. FVC is the maximum volume of air exhaled after a maximal inhalation and depends on lung elasticity, the anatomy of the thoracic cage, and respiratory muscle function. According to the American Thoracic Society (ATS), the TLC predicted (adjusted for gender, age, height) value can be used for assessing the severity of restriction: TLC < 80%: Restrictive disease 70-80% predicted: Mild restrictive disease 60-70% predicted: Moderate restrictive disease 50-60% predicted: Moderately severe restrictive disease <50% predicted: Severe restrictive disease [20] [21]

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Pathophysiology -- Functional Characteristics
content: In restrictive diseases, the forced expiratory volume over 1 second (FEV 1 ) usually results in a slight decrease or remaining normal, and the ratio of FEV 1 to FVC is generally preserved or increased. These alterations in pulmonary dynamics can be compensated for by an increased respiratory rate, with hypercapnia developing only at later stages of the disease. [22] In obstructive diseases,  TLC and FVC results are normal (80%-120% of predicted) or increased, and FEV 1 is reduced compared to FVC. In restrictive diseases, the forced expiratory volume over 1 second (FEV 1 ) usually results in a slight decrease or remaining normal, and the ratio of FEV 1 to FVC is generally preserved or increased. These alterations in pulmonary dynamics can be compensated for by an increased respiratory rate, with hypercapnia developing only at later stages of the disease. [22] In obstructive diseases,  TLC and FVC results are normal (80%-120% of predicted) or increased, and FEV 1 is reduced compared to FVC. In summary, the patterns of PFTs in the 2 groups of respiratory diseases are:

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Histopathology
content: Intrinsic interstitial diseases originate from the alveolar capillaries with protein exudation, hemorrhage, and accumulation of inflammatory elements in the alveolar spaces. Alternatively, edema and interstitial inflammatory infiltration may occur, resulting in interstitial fibrosis. Some histopathologic findings are specific to a particular disease process, while others are associated with multiple conditions.

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Histopathology -- Usual Interstitial Pneumonia and Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
content: The morphological pattern of usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) is characterized by areas of normal lung interspersed with fibrotic areas in a subpleural and paraseptal distribution. This pattern is not exclusive to IPF but can be found in rheumatoid arthritis and chronic HP. IPF is a specific form of chronic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia of unknown etiology (idiopathic UIP), in which alveolitis produces fibroblast proliferation and collagen deposition. One of the distinctive characteristics of the UIP/IPF pattern is the temporal heterogeneity of fibrosis. Dense scar areas of mature collagen fibrosis and "honeycomb" areas coexist with young fibroblastic proliferations called fibroblastic foci. Furthermore, polyploid proliferation of myofibroblasts, generally protruding into alveolar or bronchiolar cavities and characterized by a stroma with scarce collagen fibers, can be observed in IPF. The interstitial septa appear fibrotic and coated with hyperplastic type II pneumocytes or epithelium in bronchiolar metaplasia with a hyperplastic appearance. [23]

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Histopathology -- Nonspecific Interstitial Pneumonia
content: Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) has histologic and radiologic characteristics distinct from other interstitial diseases of unknown etiology. Distinguishing between the morphological characteristics is essential because NSIP has a more favorable prognosis than UIP. Morphologically, changes in lung architecture do not fully meet the criteria of other forms of interstitial lung disease. Three subgroups of the NSIP pattern are recognized: Cellular pattern: Mild to moderate chronic inflammatory interstitial infiltrate, mainly represented by lymphocytes and plasma cells, occasionally arranged in nodular aggregates Fibrous pattern: Scarce cellular elements with a greater fibrotic component Mixed pattern: Coexistence of cellular and fibrotic forms

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Histopathology -- Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia
content: The morphological pattern often shows a bronchiolocentric distribution, preserving the pulmonary architecture in areas surrounding the remodelling process. Morphological characteristics include proliferation of connective tissue (Masson bodies) inside the small airways and alveolar ducts, occlusion of the bronchioles (obliterating bronchiolitis), and surrounding alveoli (organized pneumonia).

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Histopathology -- Sarcoidosis
content: Sarcoidosis is a multisystemic inflammatory disease that almost always affects the lungs (90% of cases) with bilateral pulmonary hilar lymph node involvement and possible simultaneous parenchymal involvement. Histopathologic features include noncaseating granulomas with tightly packed epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, and T lymphocytes. These findings are localized in the interstitium adjacent to bronchioles and around and within vessel walls, pleura, and connective tissue septa. Schaumann bodies (laminated concretions of calcium and protein) and asteroid elements (stellate inclusions within giant cells) are characteristic. Parenchymal fibrosis in late stages is attributed to intrinsic restriction.

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Histopathology -- Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis
content: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP) may present as the acute/subacute nonfibrotic or the chronic fibrotic variants. The nonfibrotic type is characterised by lymphocytic infiltrates centered around bronchioles, extending into the surrounding interstitium, and poorly formed granulomas. The fibrotic HP demonstrates airway-centred fibrosis with fibroblasts, collagen deposition, and poorly formed granulomas predominantly in subpleural and centriacinar regions. The hallmark of HP is evidence of small airway disease and interstitial inflammation or fibrosis, depending on the disease stage. [24]

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- History and Physical
content: A comprehensive history and thorough physical examination are necessary to accurately identify and classify these complex disorders. The severity, onset, duration, and progression of symptoms, as well as the family, smoking, occupational, environmental exposure, and illicit substance histories, are helpful. A history of autoimmune disease can also inform the diagnosis. [3] Each particular disease has pathognomonic signs and symptoms that are unique to its pathophysiology. However, most are characterized by an insidious progression of dyspnea. [19] Moreover, ILDs classically produce the "3 Cs": cough, clubbing of the digits, and coarse crackles on auscultation. [25]

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- History and Physical
content: Patients also need to be examined for skin changes, joint swelling or deformity, alopecia, and oral ulcers suggestive of connective tissue diseases. Additional characteristics in patients with extrinsic restriction may include an elevated body mass index, spinal deviation, chest wall abnormality, muscular wasting, abnormal posture, or abdominal distension. Heart failure secondary to chronic restrictive lung disease can present with jugular venous distention and pedal edema. Clinical features and prognosis vary among the diseases. For instance, IPF involves a progressive decline in lung function that leads to eventual respiratory failure. Accordingly, the condition has a poor prognosis with a median survival of 3 to 5 years after diagnosis.

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Evaluation
content: The standard evaluation of pulmonary restriction is pulmonary function testing. Initial results indicative of pulmonary restriction include a decreased TLC with a preserved FEV 1 /FVC ratio (greater than 70%). Once a restrictive pattern is suggested on spirometry, patients should be referred for full PFTs with DLCO measurement, which is decreased in patients with intrinsic pulmonary restriction. [26] Assessment of residual volume and TLC is performed by body plethysmography, helium dilution, nitrogen washout, or radiographic methods. Please see StatPearls' companion resources, " Body Plethysmography " and " Physiology, Lung Capacity ," for more information. [27] Patients with extrinsic pulmonary restriction also present with a restrictive pattern on PFTs; however, DLCO remains within the reference range. [28] The PFT characteristics of different restrictive etiologies are summarized below in Table 2.

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Evaluation
content: Additional testing with high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the thorax, inflammatory markers, metabolic profile, diagnostic thoracentesis, abdominal ultrasonography, and specific autoantibodies should be performed according to the possible etiology. In IPF, HRCT demonstrates the typical appearance of coarse crosslinking in the basal and posterior regions in the early stages, and peripheral/subpleural "honeycomb" cystic alterations and bronchiectasis due to traction fibrosis in advanced disease. A subtype of ILD is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Guidelines from the ATS suggest considering this diagnosis in adult patients with newly detected bilateral fibrosis on a chest radiograph or CT, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, older than 60, and lung disease with unknown etiology. [21]

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Treatment / Management
content: Management of restrictive lung disease varies depending on the etiology. Patients diagnosed with IPF were historically treated with immunosuppression; however, antifibrotic drugs such as pirfenidone and nintedanib are increasingly used to slow disease progression. [29] Patients with autoimmune conditions associated with ILD, such as systemic sclerosis, are treated with immunosuppressant drugs, including corticosteroids, mycophenolate mofetil, and cyclophosphamide, depending on severity. [30] ATS uses progressive pulmonary fibrosis designation  for non-IPF fibrotic ILDs characterized by symptomatic worsening, an absolute decline in FVC by 5% or more, DLCO by 10% or more, or radiological worsening over 12 months. Objective evidence of progression in fibrotic lung diseases allows for timely revision of therapy. [23]

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Treatment / Management
content: Patients with acute exacerbations are usually treated with corticosteroids over several days; however, prolonged corticosteroid therapy is not recommended due to associated complications. [31] Oxygen therapy, management of comorbid conditions, and pulmonary rehabilitation, in addition to pirfenidone and nintedanib, are recommended in IPF. [1] [32] For patients with obesity, management involves weight loss. [3] Tirzepatide is an injectable agent that promotes insulin secretion and sensitization, leading to weight loss comparable to that achieved with bariatric surgery. [33] Patients with morbid obesity who do not lose weight with more conservative methods should be referred for gastric bypass surgery evaluation because it is effective in achieving significant weight loss and improvement in PFTs. [34]

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Treatment / Management
content: Concomitant treatment of complications such as obstructive sleep apnea and heart failure should also be pursued while awaiting significant weight reduction.  Patients with neuromuscular diseases should receive ventilatory support, including positive pressure ventilation, diaphragmatic pacing, or assistance with pneumobelts. Other supportive measures include airway clearance and respiratory muscle training. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Respiratory Muscle Strength Training ," for more information.  Chest wall disorders require surgical correction, which is most effective when performed at a young age. [35] Patients with extensive pulmonary fibrosis and chronic respiratory failure should be evaluated for lung transplantation. [36]

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis of pulmonary restriction remains broad, even after diagnosis is confirmed with PFTs. See Tables 3 and 4 below. Intrinsic pulmonary restriction may be approached based on the duration of symptoms at presentation.

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis of restrictive lung disease varies depending on the etiology. Patients with pulmonary restriction from a pleural effusion often experience resolution of symptoms with drainage of the effusion, and pregnant individuals recover with delivery. Intrinsic pulmonary restriction from nonfibrotic ILDs like cryptogenic organizing pneumonia, cellular NSIP, early-stage sarcoidosis, HP, and autoimmune disease–related ILD is associated with excellent long-term outcomes when treated. Patients diagnosed with IPF have a median survival of 3 to 5 years after diagnosis. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia ," for more information. [37] Acute interstitial pneumonia has a grave prognosis, with greater than 70% mortality within 3 months. [38]  Due to the diverse nature of restrictive lung disease, a specific diagnosis should be pursued once pulmonary restriction has been confirmed.

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Complications
content: Advanced restrictive lung disease results in hypoxemia, which is initially compensated for by an increased respiratory rate. The increased work of breathing can lead to muscle wasting and weight loss. Once compensatory mechanisms fail and hypoxia worsens, patients develop chronic respiratory failure. Sleep disorders, including obstructive sleep apnea, are common in patients with extrinsic pulmonary restriction due to obesity and also occur frequently in intrinsic restrictive lung disease. [39] Chronic respiratory failure and lung architecture distortion lead to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: After identification of the etiology of the pulmonary restriction, patients should be educated about the available treatment options. For patients with progressive disease, pulmonary rehabilitation programs offer counseling on breathing techniques and oxygen use, as well as exercises that can enhance respiratory function and alleviate symptoms. Lifestyle interventions such as exercise, weight loss, and medications can be effective, especially when obesity is the cause of pulmonary restriction.

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: The management of restrictive lung diseases is often complex and challenging due to the breadth of disease etiologies. For a primary care clinician, knowing when to refer a patient to a pulmonologist can be highly beneficial. Due to the numerous differential diagnoses and potential complications, an interdisciplinary approach is recommended. Apart from the primary care clinician and pulmonologist, the team also includes nurses who periodically assess the patient, as well as internists and intensivists providing care in the inpatient setting.

title: Restrictive Lung Disease -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Cardiology evaluation should be obtained, especially if pulmonary restriction leads to signs of heart strain or failure. Pharmacists are an essential part of the team whenever specialty medications, including antifibrotic agents, are prescribed. Nutritionists should also be included in cases of obesity, and neurologists should be involved in cases of neuromuscular disease. Transplant surgeons may assess patients with end-stage disease for a lung transplant. Palliative and hospice care specialists should be engaged in the management of terminal disease.
